title: HIS-201 Ch. 4 — 1 Definitions
subject: HIS-201
topic: Chapter 4: Colonization and Conflict in the North

cards.def: The exchange in which Indian allies supplied beaver pelts to European traders in return for European goods such as textiles, glass, copper, ironware and, later, guns.
A hat made from felt of beaver pelts, the world's best hat felt because it was sturdy, rain-resistant and lush, which made the beaver the creature at the center of the fur trade.
"Runners in the woods," French traders who lived among Indian peoples and learned their languages and customs to carry on the fur trade.
A movement by devout Catholics to correct those abuses that had prompted the Protestant Reformation.
A series of wars in which the Iroquois attacked the Hurons and dozens of other Indian peoples to win new beaver hunting grounds and captives to replace their dead.
The Calvinist idea of divine sovereignty: that an all-powerful God ordained the outcome of history, including each person's eternal fate, and directed individuals, nations and all creation.
The framework of government the Pilgrims drew up aboard the Mayflower before landing, providing a governor and assistants elected each year by Plymouth's adult males.
In Massachusetts Bay, the men entitled to vote for the governor and assistants, at first the company's stockholders and later every adult male church member.
The large wave of Puritan family migration from England to New England that ended when the English Civil War began.
John Winthrop's phrase for the godly Massachusetts Bay society he meant to build as an example to the whole world.
A genuine spiritual rebirth that a person had to convince a Puritan minister and congregation of before being admitted as a church member.
Population growth that comes from births outnumbering deaths, as in New England's low death rates and high birthrates, rather than from new immigrants.
The leader of an Algonquian village, who directed economic life, administered justice and negotiated with outsiders, and whose power depended on keeping the people's trust and consent.
Separate towns set up by the Puritan minister John Eliot for Indians who had converted to Christianity.
An annual fee for the use of the land, paid by settlers to a colony's owners.
The Quaker belief that all men and women share equally in an inner spiritual light, the root of Quaker egalitarian ideals.
William Penn's plan for Pennsylvania, which created a representative assembly and guaranteed basic English civil liberties and complete freedom of worship.
Laws passed by the English Parliament to regulate colonial trade so that it profited England, for example through customs duties on colonial tobacco.
A single royal government with a royal governor, an appointed council and no elected assemblies, combining the New England colonies and later New York and New Jersey.

The quick, bloodless coup in which Parliament forced the Catholic Stuart king James II into exile and raised his daughter Mary and her Dutch husband William of Orange to the throne, and Mary agreed to rule with Parliament.
Colonial courts without juries, run by royally appointed judges, that prosecuted smugglers.
A colony whose governor, and usually its council, were appointed by the monarch.
